extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and advanced students interested in the nature of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for (1) when a scientific community accepts or rejects a paradigm, (2) what counts as scientific progress, and (3) the social/professional features that enable scientific growth. The page discusses what a candidate paradigm must provide and what characterizes scientific communities that produce cumulative results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of an outstanding problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The new candidate must seem to resolve some outstanding and generally recognized problem that can be met in no other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes that one decisive desideratum for accepting a new paradigm is its ability to solve a recognized anomaly that the old paradigm cannot handle. This criterion is presented as necessary for persuading the community to adopt the new view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of prior problem-solving ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The new paradigm must promise to preserve a relatively large part of the concrete problem-solving ability that has accrued to science through its predecessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty for its own sake is not valued; successful paradigms typically retain many concrete capabilities of prior paradigms while permitting additional problem-solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior crisis as precondition for change
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior crisis is important: scientists who have not experienced crisis will seldom renounce the hard evidence of problem-solving to follow a new paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues that without a crisis that undermines confidence in the existing paradigm, the profession will not accept a candidate that threatens solved problems. Crisis makes room for faith in a new paradigm's promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence and activity of early supporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Early adopters must be competent, will improve the candidate, explore its possibilities, and show what it would be like to belong to the community guided by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion depends on competent advocates who develop the paradigm into workable practice—producing experiments, instruments, articles, and books that demonstrate its fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple persuasive arguments; gradual shift of allegiances
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single argument that can or should persuade all scientists; persuasion occurs by an increasing shift in the distribution of professional allegiances as arguments accumulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn stresses that acceptance is social and cumulative—many arguments, not one decisive proof, convert the community over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of non-rational appeals (aesthetic/personal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes personal and inarticulate aesthetic considerations provide the initial basis for faith in a new proposal, converting some men when articulable technical arguments point the other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such appeals are acknowledged as real but rarely sufficient alone; they can seed early support until hardheaded arguments can be produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of scientific achievement: solved problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of scientific achievement is the solved problem; scientific progress is measured by the number and precision of problems the community solves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn uses solved problems as the metric for growth: as paradigms define puzzles to be solved, their solution increases the discipline's accumulated, precise knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulation and peer evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mature scientific communities are unusually insulated from lay demands and evaluate work primarily by professional peers who share the same standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This insulation permits concentration on problems deemed solvable with available tools and enables a single set of standards to be taken for granted—key conditions for efficient progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational initiation geared to normal science
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific education relies heavily on textbooks that recapitulate established results, equipping students for normal (puzzle-solving) science rather than for discovering radically new approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbook-centered initiation makes practitioners efficient at working within paradigms but less prepared to invent fresh paradigms; nevertheless, this training supports community-wide problem-solving efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the professional community
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to choose between paradigms must be vested in the members of the scientific community rather than in heads of state or the populace at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn asserts an unwritten rule against appeals to nonprofessional authority in scientific matters; a uniquely competent professional group must be the exclusive arbiter of professional achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership criteria for a scientific community
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists should be concerned to solve problems about the behavior of nature, focus on problems of detail, and require that solutions be accepted by many professional peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features distinguish scientific communities from other professional groups and underlie the community's ability to evaluate and sustain cumulative problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of losses from revolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific revolutions bring gains and losses: they may banish many books/articles embodying the old paradigm, narrow the scope of professional concerns, increase specialization, and attenuate communication with other groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn warns historians and scientists that communities often become blind to the losses of revolution; recognition of losses is necessary for a balanced assessment of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress as evolution-from-known, not toward fixed truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific development may be evolutionary from the community's current knowledge rather than movement toward a single, fixed, objective 'truth'; there need be no one pre-set goal of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn invites substituting 'evolution-from-what-we-do-know' for 'evolution-toward-what-we-wish-to-know', which reframes induction problems and the meaning of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-shared rules for judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The group must be seen as possessing shared rules of the game or an equivalent basis for unequivocal judgments; otherwise incompatible standards would undermine the unity of scientific truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A shared evaluative basis is required to prevent incompatible standards of achievement and to sustain a coherent science; this social cohesion is itself a criterion for a functioning scientific community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of paradigms through intra-community conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigm selection is effected by conflict within the scientific community; the victorious practice is the 'fittest' way to practice future science, akin to selection in biological evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn draws the analogy to natural selection: repeated revolutionary selections, separated by normal science, yield the adapted body of modern scientific knowledge without implying goal-directed progress.
